metadata.title: Multilevel analysis of the effects of principal support and innovative school climate on the integration of technology in learning activities

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study collected survey responses from 364 teachers nested in 17 schools in Serbia (primary and secondary schools). The methodology describes multilevel modeling (random intercepts/slopes, restricted maximum likelihood, Kenward–Roger correction) but does not report the use of any complex survey sampling weights or replicate weights. Because the analysis is based on a small, purposively recruited set of participating schools/teachers rather than an international probability sample, the manuscript does not specify any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and no replicate-weight procedure (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is mentioned. The main preprocessing described concerns scale translation/back-translation and centering (cluster-mean centering for level-1 predictors and grand-mean centering for school-level predictors), rather than weight-based estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use ILSA cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it models teacher-reported Likert-scale constructs (principal support, innovative climate) and technology-use frequency subscales from the ICAP-TS. Because the dependent variables are not PV-based achievement scores, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe a missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), so missing-data handling is not reported.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample comprised 364 teachers from 17 primary and secondary schools across Serbia. Schools were recruited via prior collaboration and participated voluntarily; teachers could complete the survey either online (Google Forms) or paper-and-pencil. The paper does not report additional exclusion criteria (e.g., minimum response completeness, item-level missingness thresholds) or any further subsampling by grade/subject beyond describing the Serbian teaching-level categories (grades 1–4, 5–8, 9–12 vocational, 9–12 grammar).

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICILS 2018 the study leveraged Principal support, Innovative school climate to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study uses Serbian teacher survey data (364 teachers in 17 schools) to validate the ICAP-TS scale and to examine multilevel associations between school context and four types of technology integration in learning activities (passive, active, constructive, interactive). The technology-use outcomes are measured with a 12-item ICAP-TS (five-point Likert frequency: 0=almost never to 4=almost every lesson), while principal support and innovative climate are measured with Likert-type scales. The authors used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) for construct validity and multilevel modeling with random intercepts (and attempted random slopes) to separate within-school and between-school variance. For passive use, principal support showed a positive within-school effect (γ10=0.164, p=.025) and innovative climate was also positive (γ20=0.224, p=.001), but in the final random-slope specification principal support became non-significant while innovative climate remained significant (γ20=0.219, p=.002). For active, constructive, and interactive use, innovative climate was consistently significant within schools (e.g., active: γ20=0.372, p<.001; interactive: γ20=0.393, p<.05), whereas principal support was not consistently significant. Limitations include the absence of a reported missing-data strategy and the fact that the study is correlational (no causal identification). This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification study: it uses CFA and multilevel (mixed-effects) modeling to validate measurement and estimate within-/between-school associations. Therefore, there are no ML algorithms, no PV-based achievement outcomes, and no predictive performance metrics to populate main_findings. The extraction leaves ml_techniques empty and main_findings as an empty array because the study’s core analyses are psychometric and multilevel regression rather than ML.
